## **Lower copper grades, not just a hidden problem** 

During July and August, Escondida’s Laguna Seca SAG mill has been under a 45-day stoppage in order for repairs to be undertaken.  This SAG mill problem combined with lower copper grades are the reasons for a 37% drop in Escondida’s copper in concentrate production in Q2 2009.  Lower grades have been the topic of many news stories, however, the Escondida deposit is a geological rarity with higher copper grades than typical across South America, it should therefore not be used as an indication for more general grade decline across the continent. 

The situation around Escondida has stimulated discussions over high grading at copper operations as a reaction to the copper price slump and to a general long run decline of copper ore grades around the world including at South American mines.  To analyse whether this is happening or not we have put together data for copper ore grades from a sample of mines and analysed them  in a similar way as we did in the July 2009 Copper Quarterly for 41 operations world wide.  For South America we focus on 22 operations (including oxides and sulphides) at 18 mines (a mine can have circuits for both sulphide and oxide ores). We have used simple averages.  Historical data enables us to go as far back as 2003 in order to maintain a representative sample.  Our key findings are: 

- Escondida’s grade is above the average in major South American mines. Even in Q1 2009, when sulphide ore grades at Escondia were the lowest quarterly average over the past ten years, it was still above the region’s average. 

- In Q2 2009 less than 20% of copper operations reported copper grades higher than their averages over the past five years.  This gives an indication that there has been no high grading. 

- The average copper grade in South America, in our sample of operations has been declining over the past five years.  This decline, however, has not been even and oxide operations have suffered the most.

## **Escondida’s low copper grades** 

In its Q3 2008 production report, BHP Billiton announced that the Escondida –meaning “Hidden” in English – mine in Chile was affected by declining ore grades and poor reliability of the Laguna Seca SAG mill motor.  On average, low grades at Escondida were mined all through Q1 2009.  Despite this declining trend, Escondida’s sulphide grades have been Escondida’s ore grades vs the well above the region’s average and, in fact, in Q2 2009 South American average they have shown a recovery. simple average of copper grades, 2003-2009 

According to data from BHP Billiton and Rio Tinto quarterly production reports, the sulphide copper ore grade at Escondida declined from its quarterly average record of the last five years of 1.72% Cu (Q4 2007) to its lowest of 0.92% Cu (Q1 2009) and recovered to 1.22% Cu in Q2 2009.  Even at its l

owest point, Escondida’s sulphide ore grade remained above the region’s average. Meanwhile, Escondida’s oxide ore grade has been below the regions average since Q3 2004. According to the latest data available from Rio Tinto, the lowest quarterly oxide grade at Escondida was 0.25% Cu in Q3 2006. No oxide grades have been reported in 2009. 1.80

South America, the Q2 2009 results show that only 3 copper operations (out of 22) reported average copper grades above their last five year averages and one was at its historical level. All others had lower than average copper grades. This suggests that copper mines were not mining areas with higher copper grades as a reaction to the decline of the copper price. In fact, it indicates that most mines may be facing lower grades as 14 operations of our sample had copper grades in Q2 2009 of at least 20% lower than their historical averages. © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 6 **August 2009** www.crumonitor.com ## **Q2 2009 ore grades showed a recovery, but the long run trend is still declining** It is a well-know fact that copper grades in South America, as well as in many other regions of the world, are showing a long run decline. This is a fact of life as

all mines have finite reserves and resources. We have classified our sample of 22 copper operations into 9 sulphides (producing copper in concentrates) and 13 oxides (producing EW cathode). In Q1 2005, for example, sulphide grades were 0.19% Cu higher than oxides ones, in Q4 2007 the same gap was 0.30% Cu and in Q2 2009 it was 0.21% Cu. # Copper production - In Chile, copper production decreased 3% y-o-y in May. This is the eleventh consecutive month of decline. The reasons are similar to those in April and March. Escondida alone produced 32,800t less because of technical failures at its Laguna Seca mill and lower ore grades. Codelco produced 18,600t more than in May 2008 mainly because of the debottlenecking at El Teniente (8,100t increase in May) and the ramp-up at Gaby (although its May production was its lowest since August 2008). All other operations in Chile remained at the same range. If Escondida had produced at the same level as in April 2008, the country’s copper output would have increased by 7%. In June, according to the National Statistics Institute, copper production in Chile was 467,185t (2.6% lower than June 2008). - In Peru, copper production increased 2%y-o-y in June. As in previous months, the ramp-up at Cerro Corona (3.1kt more than in June 2008) offset the decline at Antamina (-3.3kt, higher zinc grades and lower copper ones). Higher production at Tintaya (1.0kt of copper in concentrates and 0.5kt of copper cathode) offset minor declines at other operations. © 2009 CRU International
